facts.claim: Ilya Repin's 'Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks' (Zaporozhian Cossacks), oil on canvas, 203 × 358 cm, 1880–1891, State Russian Museum, St Petersburg (inv. Ж-4005); it depicts the legendary insulting reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks, led by Ataman Ivan Sirko, to Sultan Mehmed IV
The legend is set in the 1670s (Wikipedia: 1676; the museum: 1675); the sultan demanded the Cossacks submit, and they replied with an insulting, profane letter

The Zaporozhian Cossacks lived 'beyond the rapids' of the Dnieper (the origin of the name), as free men on the steppe frontier, defending against the Crimean Tatars; their numbers grew with peasants fleeing serfdom; their councils and otamans were elected
Mehmed IV became sultan in 1648 at the age of six; under him the Ottoman Empire reached its greatest territorial extent in Europe; his army besieged Vienna in 1683

In the widely circulated text the sultan lists grandiose titles and orders the Cossacks to submit 'voluntarily and without any resistance'; the reply calls him (in one translation) 'Babylonian scullion, Macedonian wheelwright, brewer of Jerusalem' and worse, and is dated by the moon because they have no calendar

Historians regard the correspondence as apocryphal: no reliable evidence it happened; its versions differ in dates, signatories and recipients; Waugh traced how the text changed in the 18th century; it belongs to a family of fake letters attributed to the sultan (translated from Dutch and German newsletters, anti-Turkish pamphlets)
Copies kept being made by hand (e.g. a manuscript dated 1733 in the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, 19th-century copies); Repin said that 'in Little Russia every sexton has a copy of this apocrypha'

In summer 1878 Repin was at Savva Mamontov's Abramtsevo estate near Moscow, where he heard the story and made his first pencil sketch (dated 26 June or 26 July 1878, sources differ), during/after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78
Savva Mamontov, railway industrialist and patron, hosted artists at Abramtsevo

Repin was born in 1844 in Chuguyev (Chuhuiv), Kharkiv province, today Ukraine; he knew the Cossack letter from his youth there; he illustrated Gogol's Taras Bulba (1872); he said of the Cossacks 'Gogol wrote about them for good reason, it's all true!'

In spring 1880 Repin travelled to the Zaporizhzhia region with the young Valentin Serov (born January 1865, so 15), visiting Khortytsia and the Dnieper rapids and the collector Vasyl Tarnovsky at Kachanivka, who showed him his collection of Cossack antiquities; Serov's 1880 Cossack drawings are in the Russian Museum
The first Zaporozhian Sich was built c. 1552 on (Mala) Khortytsia island
Repin studied Cossack weapons and clothing and sketched objects of Cossack life

In October 1880 Leo Tolstoy discussed the study with Repin in his Moscow studio and advised a broader picture expressing the spirit of the people rather than a small incident; Repin enlarged the composition and added figures
Repin to Stasov, 6 November 1880 (translation printed by W. K. Lang): 'No one on this earth has felt liberty, equality and fraternity as deeply as they!'

The figures were painted from real people Repin knew; the scribe is the historian Dmytro Yavornytsky (Evarnitsky), Repin's consultant, whom Repin met in 1887; he was reluctant to pose and Repin got his expression by showing him a magazine of caricatures
Ataman Ivan Sirko was modelled on General Mikhail Dragomirov, commander of the Kiev Military District (spring 1889); Repin reportedly exclaimed 'A living Sirko!'
Anecdote (told as a story): Dragomirov forgot Alexander III's name day and two days later telegraphed 'For the third day we've been drinking to Your Majesty's health'
Fyodor Stravinsky, Mariinsky opera singer and father of Igor Stravinsky, posed for one of the Cossacks (per Repin's 1926 recollection)

Georgy Alekseyev, an imperial court official, refused to let Repin sketch the back of his bald head; Yavornytsky distracted him with his coin collection while Repin drew; Repin reportedly said 'It takes centuries to create a head like that!'

Other models: the collector Vasyl Tarnovsky as the judge; his coachman as the Cossack Holota; Professor Alexander Rubets; the teacher Kostiantyn Belonovsky; a student; and an old man Repin met on a pier at Alexandrovsk (Zaporizhzhia)

Repin repeatedly set the painting aside for other works: Religious Procession in Kursk Province (1880–83), Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan (1885), Saint Nicholas Saves Three Innocents from Death (1888)
Alexander III banned the exhibition of Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan in 1885 (lifted after about three months)
In 1888 Repin travelled to the Caucasus/Kuban (stanitsa Pashkovskaya) to study descendants of the Zaporozhian Cossacks
Repin finished in 1891 and recorded the years along the lower edge with his signature ('И.Репин 1880-91', bottom centre)
Critical reception was mixed: Alexandre Benois called it 'a coarse and ridiculous spectacle'; Nikolai Ghe faulted its lack of idealism
Alexander III bought the painting for 35,000 rubles, an enormous sum for the time; it hung in the Winter Palace until 1897, when Nicholas II gave it to the Russian Museum

The last Zaporozhian Sich was destroyed by a Russian army on 15–16 June 1775, in the reign of Catherine II; Alexander III was her great-great-grandson (Catherine → Paul I → Nicholas I → Alexander II → Alexander III)
Repin wrote to Yavornytsky that the tsar had bought his Zaporozhians: 'Hurrah!'
With the 35,000 rubles Repin bought the estate of Zdravnevo near Vitebsk (May 1892), where he spent summers until about 1900–1902
The painting won gold medals at the 1895 international exhibitions in Munich and Budapest

Repin began a second, more 'historically authentic/accurate' version in 1889 (dated 1893); in 1932 it went from the Tretyakov Gallery to Kharkiv, and since 1935 it is in the Kharkiv Art Museum; in it the scribe is older and wears spectacles
In 1907 Repin donated his portrait of General Dragomirov to the Kharkiv museum (then the City Art and Industry Museum)
In March 2022 Russian shelling shattered the Kharkiv Art Museum's windows; staff took the second version of the Cossacks off the wall and moved it to safety
On 14 June 2026 a Russian drone strike set the Kharkiv Art Museum on fire; Repin's second version of the Cossacks survived
Yavornytsky later toasted Repin at a dinner in his honour, thanking him for making Cossack history known: 'We were small, close to the ground; now we stand a head taller'
Since 2014 Ukrainian soldiers have restaged the painting in photographs (Yuriy Bilak, Donbas 2015; 2022; Emeric Lhuisset 2023; 53rd Brigade 2024)

titles: These Men Are Laughing at an Emperor
A Tsar Paid a Fortune for This Insult
youtube.description_lead: Ilya Repin spent eleven years (1880–1891) painting the Zaporozhian Cossacks writing their legendary, very rude reply to the Ottoman sultan Mehmed IV, a letter that historians think was probably never written as we know it. Almost every laughing face is a real person Repin knew: the historian Dmytro Yavornytsky is the scribe, General Mikhail Dragomirov is the ataman Ivan Sirko, the opera bass Fyodor Stravinsky is somewhere in the crowd, and a court official who refused to pose lent the back of his bald head without knowing it. Tsar Alexander III paid 35,000 rubles for the painting. Repin's second version survives in Kharkiv, Ukraine.
